On 8 Aug 2016, at 23:00, Gustavo Machado <gusta...@gmail.com> wrote:
Thank you very much, yes I have a discuss with people that are in MCMC but since we have this large data we can not fit in BUGS.

That's not what I meant. What I meant was that the entire concept of "check the model fit by looking at the mcmc trace plots to see if the MCMC chain has converged and is mixing well" is a question about an MCMC algorithm, and is not a relevant question when using the INLA method for Bayesian inference, so if someone requests that for INLA they most likely do not understand what INLA does, and/or that "Bayesian" is not synonymous with "MCMC".
How could I get in this place the the optimization (residuals and gradient) from the model above? in order to converse my college that my model is doing ok?

The optimization diagnostics can be found in the verbose output; look for lines with "gradient" for example. But that only tells you something if you know how numerical optimization works, and doesn't usually tell you much at all about if your model fit is ok.

So, are you looking for evidence showing that the numerical algorithm has converged to the correct answer to the stated question (the posterior distributions for your specified model), or evidence that your model-data fit is good? Those are two very different questions, and the answer to the first one can be "yes" at the same time as the answer to the second question is "no" (the reverse can also happen, but is rare, and if it happens the results should generally not be trusted, since it is then unclear which question the algorithm has provided an answer to).

Finn

The optimization diagnostics can be found in the verbose output; look for lines with "gradient" for example. But that only tells you something if you know how numerical optimization works, and doesn't usually tell you much at all about if your model fit is ok.

So, are you looking for evidence showing that the numerical algorithm has converged to the correct answer to the stated question (the posterior distributions for your specified model), or evidence that your model-data fit is good? Those are two very different questions, and the answer to the first one can be "yes" at the same time as the answer to the second question is "no" (the reverse can also happen, but is rare, and if it happens the results should generally not be trusted, since it is then unclear which question the algorithm has provided an answer to).

Trace plot? 

It sounds like you're asking for something that would be relevant for an MCMC run, and not a direct calculation like INLA. That said, the optimization step of INLA is the closest relative of that, and convergence to the mode is checked as part of the termination for the numerical optimization algorithm. Does that fit with what you need?

That's not what I meant. What I meant was that the entire concept of "check the model fit by looking at the mcmc trace plots to see if the MCMC chain has converged and is mixing well" is a question about an MCMC algorithm, and is not a relevant question when using the INLA method for Bayesian inference, so if someone requests that for INLA they most likely do not understand what INLA does, and/or that "Bayesian" is not synonymous with "MCMC".

How could I get in this place the the optimization (residuals and gradient) from the model above? in order to converse my college that my model is doing ok?

The optimization diagnostics can be found in the verbose output; look for lines with "gradient" for example. But that only tells you something if you know how numerical optimization works, and doesn't usually tell you much at all about if your model fit is ok.

So, are you looking for evidence showing that the numerical algorithm has converged to the correct answer to the stated question (the posterior distributions for your specified model), or evidence that your model-data fit is good? Those are two very different questions, and the answer to the first one can be "yes" at the same time as the answer to the second question is "no" (the reverse can also happen, but is rare, and if it happens the results should generally not be trusted, since it is then unclear which question the algorithm has provided an answer to).

Finn
